messages.content: How many piano tuners are there in a city of about a million people? I have no idea where to even start.

Start by chaining quantities you can reason about, and keep every assumption explicit so the estimate can be audited.

Population 1,000,000, at about 2.5 people per household, gives 400,000 households. Suppose 5% of households own a piano: 20,000 pianos. A piano gets tuned about once a year, so the city needs roughly 20,000 tunings per year.

Now the supply side: a tuner who also drives between jobs manages about 3 tunings a day, 240 working days a year, so 720 tunings per tuner per year. Divide demand by supply: 20,000 / 720 is about 28.

Sanity check: if the piano-ownership rate were 2% instead of 5%, the answer drops to about 11; if 10%, it rises to about 56. So the honest answer is 'a few dozen, order of magnitude tens' — and that range, not a fake-precise single number, is what a good Fermi estimate delivers.
Roughly how many golf balls would fit inside a school bus?

Estimate the container, estimate the object, then correct for wasted space.

A school bus interior is about 11 m long, 2.4 m wide, and 1.9 m of usable height: about 50 cubic metres. A golf ball is 4.27 cm across, so its volume is 4/3 pi r^3, about 41 cubic centimetres. Spheres poured into a box only fill about 64% of the space (random packing), so each ball effectively costs 64 cubic centimetres.

Divide: 50 / 0.00006 gives roughly 787,509 balls. Seats and the driver's cab would eat into that, so call it several hundred thousand — the order of magnitude is 10^6, and any answer between about 300,000 and 1,000,000 rests on defensible assumptions.
How many hairs are on a typical human head? Give me a way to estimate it, not just a number you looked up.

Build it from area times density. The hair-bearing part of the scalp is roughly 550 square centimetres — picture the top and back of the head as a patch about 25 cm by 22 cm. Hair follicles are packed at roughly 180 per square centimetre on average (denser in some spots, thinner at the hairline).

Multiply: 550 x 180 is about 99,000, so roughly 100,000 hairs. That matches what dermatology references report (about 100,000 follicles, varying by natural hair colour), which is the sanity check: two independent routes landing in the same place. The method matters more than the digit — if your density guess is off by a factor of two, you still land in the right order of magnitude, and you know exactly which assumption to argue about.
About how many times does a person's heart beat in a lifetime?

Pick a defensible average rate and multiply through the time units. A resting heart rate is around 60-70 bpm, exercise pushes it far higher, sleep lower; 72 bpm is a reasonable all-day average.

Per day: 72 x 60 x 24 = 103,680 beats. Per year: x 365.25 = about 37.9 million. Over 80 years: about 3.0 billion beats.

Sanity check the scale: a billion seconds is about 31.7 years, so 'a few billion heartbeats per lifetime' and 'about one beat per second on average' tell the same story. The answer is robust: even at 60 bpm for 75 years you get 2.4 billion — same order of magnitude, which is all an estimate like this promises.
If someone wanted to fill books with everything they say in a lifetime, how many novels' worth of words would that be?

Estimate the daily flow first. Studies of everyday speech put people at roughly 15,000 words spoken per day (estimates range from about 13,000 to 16,000, with big individual variation).

Per lifetime: 15,000 x 365 days x 75 years is about 411 million words. A typical novel runs about 90,000 words, so divide: 410,625,000 / 90,000 is roughly 4,562 novels.

Sanity check by a second route: 16 waking hours at, say, 20% of the time actually talking and 150 words per minute gives 16 x 60 x 0.20 x 150 = 28,800 words a day — same ballpark, a bit higher. Two crude methods bracketing the answer is exactly what you want before trusting a Fermi estimate.
Estimate the number of gas stations in the United States from scratch.

Work from demand: how many fill-ups happen per day, and how many can one station serve?

There are roughly 260 million vehicles on US roads. If the average vehicle fills up about once every 10 days, that is 26 million fill-ups per day. A station with 8 pumps, each handling a fill-up roughly every 12 minutes over a busy 8-hour core and slower the rest of the day, might serve about 320 fill-ups daily.

Divide: 26,000,000 / 320 is about 81,250 stations — order of magnitude 10^5. The real count is around 150,000 including small convenience-store pumps, so the estimate lands within a factor of two. The gap is instructive: many real stations serve far fewer than 320 cars a day, which tells you the average station in the estimate is busier than the average station in reality. Naming that discrepancy is part of the craft.
A coffee chain wants to know roughly how many cups of coffee are bought (not made at home) each day in a city of 500,000 people. Estimate it.

Chain the fractions, keeping each one visible. Adults are about 75% of the population: 375,000. Suppose 60% of adults drink coffee daily: 225,000 drinkers. At an average of 2 cups a day, that is 450,000 cups consumed.

Now the key cut: most coffee is made at home or at work. If about 25% of cups are bought at a shop, the purchased volume is about 112,500 cups per day.

Sanity check from the supply side: if the city has around 250 coffee shops and cafes, that is 450 purchased cups per shop per day — busy but plausible for a mix of chains and small cafes. If your shop count or cups-per-shop feels off, adjust that assumption; the structure of the estimate stays the same.
How would you estimate the number of leaves on a big oak tree without counting them all?

Use the tree's branching structure: count at one small scale, then multiply up level by level.

A large oak might have about 12 main limbs. Each limb carries roughly 8 secondary branches, and each of those about 25 small twigs: 12 x 8 x 25 = 2,400 twigs. If a twig holds about 60 leaves, the total is about 144,000 leaves.

Every factor here is uncertain by maybe 50%, and the errors multiply, so quote the result as an order of magnitude: around 10^5 leaves, plausibly anywhere from 50,000 to 400,000. A useful cross-check is sampling: photograph one dense section of canopy, count leaves in a known fraction of the crown's volume, and scale up — if both routes give 10^5, you can plan around it (for example, estimating leaf-litter volume in autumn).
How long would it take to count out loud to a million?

The trap is assuming one second per number. Short numbers take about a second, but 'seven hundred forty-three thousand, two hundred sixteen' takes three or four. A fair average across the whole run is about 2.5 seconds per number.

Total: 2.5 x 1,000,000 = 2,500,000 seconds, which is 29 days of nonstop counting. At a sustainable 12 hours a day, double it: about 58 days, roughly two months.

Sanity check the shape of the answer: counting to a thousand at the same pace takes about 40 minutes, which matches most people's experience of such stunts. Estimation is often just unit conversion done honestly — the only real judgment call was the 2.5-second average, and the final answer scales directly with it.
Estimate how many elevator trips happen per day in a 40-storey office tower with about 5,000 occupants.

Count person-rides first, then convert to trips. A typical occupant rides about 4 times a day: up in the morning, down and back up around lunch, down at the end of the day. That is 20,000 person-rides.

Elevators rarely run full; at an average of 8 passengers per loaded trip, that is 2,500 loaded trips. Add roughly 30% for empty repositioning runs (cars returning to the lobby, answering calls on the way), giving about 3,250 trips per day across the building.

Sanity check: spread over a bank of 10 elevators and a 10-hour busy window, that is 325 trips per elevator, or one trip every 111 seconds — brisk but believable for a tower at rush hours. The estimate also tells management something useful: the morning peak, when most of the 20,000 rides compress into one hour, is what actually sizes the system.

A two-storey house measures 40 ft by 30 ft with exterior walls 18 ft high. Windows and doors take up about 15% of the wall area. A standard brick plus its mortar joint covers a face 8.5 in by 2.75 in. Estimate the number of bricks in the outer walls (single brick thickness). Show the estimate in steps.

Assumptions: rectangular footprint, single-wythe brick veneer, 15% openings.

Step 1, wall area: perimeter 2 x (40 + 30) = 140 ft; times 18 ft height = 2,520 sq ft.
Step 2, subtract openings: 2,520 x 0.85 = 2,142 sq ft of actual brickwork.
Step 3, bricks per square foot: one brick face is 8.5 x 2.75 = 23.4 sq in = 0.162 sq ft, so about 6.2 bricks per sq ft.
Step 4, total: 2,142 x 6.2 = about 13,196 bricks.

Order of magnitude 10^4. Add a few percent for cuts and breakage if ordering. The biggest lever in the estimate is wall height, not the brick size — a one-storey version of the same house needs barely half as many.
There's a 2-litre jar of jellybeans at a fair. How do you come up with a serious guess for the count?

Convert the problem into volumes. The jar holds 2 litres = 2,000 cubic centimetres of space. A jellybean is about 2 cm long and 1.3 cm thick; as a rounded solid it occupies roughly 1.7 cubic centimetres, but poured beans leave air gaps — with a packing fraction around 0.6, each bean effectively consumes about 3 cubic centimetres of jar.

Divide: 2,000 / 3 gives about 667 beans. Quote it as 'roughly 600-700' rather than a single digit-perfect number, because the packing assumption dominates the error.

If the fair lets you handle the jar, a second route sharpens it: count the beans visible in a measured patch of the jar's side, estimate how many layers deep the jar is, and multiply. Two independent estimates that agree within 20% are worth far more than one clever one.
An American football field, including end zones, is 120 yards long and 53.3 yards wide. One inch of rain falls on it. Compute how many gallons of water that is, showing the unit conversions.

Step 1, area: 120 yd x 53.3 yd = 6,396 sq yd. In feet: 360 ft x 160 ft = about 57,564 sq ft.
Step 2, volume: 1 inch is 1/12 ft, so volume = 57,564 / 12 = about 4,797 cubic feet.
Step 3, gallons: 1 cubic foot = 7.48 gallons, so 4,797 x 7.48 = about 35,884 gallons.

Sanity check: an acre-inch of water is a known irrigation unit, about 27,154 gallons. The field is about 1.32 acres, and 1.32 x 27,154 = 35,843 gallons — same answer by a second route. One inch of rain is a far bigger delivery of water than intuition suggests: roughly 60 backyard swimming pools at 600 gallons each.
Roughly how many steps would it take to walk across the United States, and how long would it take?

A coast-to-coast walking route is about 4,300 km (routes vary; the American Discovery Trail is longer, a direct-ish road route shorter). An adult's stride is about 0.8 m, so the step count is 4,300,000 / 0.8 = about 5.4 million steps.

For duration: a fit walker sustaining 30 km a day — a solid but not heroic pace — needs 4,300 / 30 = about 143 walking days, call it five months with rest days included.

Sanity check: 30 km at 0.8 m per step is 37,500 steps a day, which matches what long-distance hikers actually log. The two halves of the estimate corroborate each other, which is what you want before quoting either.
Give me an order-of-magnitude estimate for how many emails are sent worldwide each day.

Build from the user base. About 5.5 billion people use the internet. Suppose half of them send at least one email on a given day, and an active sender averages about 20 sent messages (work threads, replies, receipts they trigger): 2.75 billion senders x 20 = about 55 billion human-initiated emails per day.

That is the floor, not the total: automated mail — notifications, marketing, machine alerts, spam — multiplies it several times over, pushing the true figure into the low hundreds of billions, order of magnitude 10^11 per day. Industry measurements of roughly 350 billion a day sit comfortably in that band.

The lesson of this estimate is to state which quantity you estimated. 'Emails people deliberately send' (~10^11) and 'messages mail servers process' (a few x 10^11) differ by a factor of three, and confusing them is how order-of-magnitude answers go wrong even when the arithmetic is fine.
Estimate how many photographs are taken worldwide in a year.

Start with cameras: there are roughly 4 billion people who regularly take photos on phones. If the average active photographer takes about 2.5 photos a day — many take none on a given day, some take dozens — the daily total is 10 billion.

Per year: 10,000,000,000 x 365 = about 3.6 trillion photos. Industry estimates for recent years run around 2 trillion annually, so this Fermi chain lands within a factor of two — respectable for three guessed inputs.

Which input is shakiest? The 2.5 photos per day: it hides a skewed distribution where a minority of heavy users take most of the pictures. If the true average were 1.5, the total drops to about 2.2 trillion. Reporting the estimate as 'order 10^12, plausibly 2-4 trillion' is the honest format.
How many grains of rice are in a 1 kg bag? Estimate it from the weight of one grain.

A single long-grain rice kernel weighs roughly 22 milligrams (you can check the scale: 50 grains on a kitchen scale read about 1.1 grams). A kilogram is 1,000,000 milligrams, so the count is 1,000,000 / 22 = about 45,455 grains.

So the answer is on the order of 45,000 grains per kilogram — a useful calibration fact. It also powers quick follow-ups: a 60 g serving of dry rice is about 2,727 grains, and the classic 'grains of rice on a chessboard' numbers become graspable because you now have a feel for what 10^4 grains looks like in a bag.
Roughly how much air does a person breathe over a whole lifetime? Express it in something I can picture.

Resting breathing is about 14 breaths a minute. Per day: 14 x 60 x 24 = 20,160 breaths. Over 80 years: 20,160 x 365.25 x 80 = about 589 million breaths.

Each resting breath moves about half a litre, so total air is 589,075,200 x 0.5 litres = about 294,538 cubic metres. An Olympic swimming pool holds about 2,500 cubic metres of water, so a lifetime of breathing is the air volume of roughly 118 Olympic pools.

Caveat worth stating: exercise raises both rate and depth several-fold, so the true figure is higher — this is a resting-rate floor. Good estimates name their direction of bias.
People say a billion is hard to grasp. If I spent $1,000 every single day, how long would a billion dollars last?

Divide it out: 1,000,000,000 / 1,000 = 1,000,000 days. Convert: / 365.25 = about 2,738 years. Spending a thousand dollars daily, a billion dollars outlasts you by millennia — you would have to start around the fall of Rome.

Contrast with a million: $1,000 a day exhausts it in 1,000 days, under three years. A billion is not 'a big million'; it is a thousand millions, and time-spending analogies expose the gap better than any string of zeros. This is the core order-of-magnitude skill: translate an abstract count into a rate-times-time you can feel, and check whether the answer changes the decision the number was supposed to inform.
How many pizzas does a town of 60,000 people eat in a year? I want two independent estimates that check each other.

Route 1, demand side: suppose the average resident eats pizza about once a month (some weekly, some never). That is 60,000 x 12 = 720,000 pizzas a year.

Route 2, supply side: suppose the town supports about 25 pizza outlets (chains, independents, and pizza counters). A modest outlet sells about 80 pizzas a day and operates 360 days a year: 25 x 80 x 360 = 720,000 pizzas.

The two routes agree exactly at 720,000 — that is partly luck (both were tuned to plausible mid-range assumptions), but agreement within a factor of two between a demand chain and a supply chain is the standard Fermi cross-check. When the routes disagree by 10x, one of your assumptions is broken and the disagreement tells you where to dig. When they agree, quote the shared order of magnitude with confidence and the point value with humility.

A store offers a $120 extended warranty on a $600 washing machine. There's about a 15% chance it'll need a repair costing around $250 during the warranty period. Is the warranty worth it on pure numbers?

Compare the certain price with the expected cost of going without. Expected repair cost without the warranty: 0.15 x $250 = $37.50. The warranty costs $120 for certain — more than three times the expected loss it protects against.

The store can price it this way because it sells thousands of warranties and the law of large numbers makes its outcome nearly certain; you own one machine, so your outcome is lumpy: most likely you pay $120 for nothing, with a 15% chance it saves you $130 net.

That doesn't make buying it irrational — if a surprise $250 bill would genuinely hurt, you're buying peace of mind and budget certainty, not a good bet. Just name it correctly: insurance against volatility, priced well above its expected value.

A lottery ticket costs $2. The jackpot is $8 million with odds of 1 in 12 million, there's a $50,000 prize at 1 in 500,000, and the small prizes are worth about $0.25 per ticket on average. What's a ticket actually worth?

Add up each prize times its probability — that sum is the expected value, the fair price of the ticket.

Jackpot: $8,000,000 x (1/12,000,000) = $0.67. Second prize: $50,000 x (1/500,000) = $0.10. Small prizes: $0.25. Total expected value: about $1.02.

You pay $2.00 for about $1.02 of expected winnings — the lottery keeps roughly half of every dollar, one of the worst payout rates in legal gambling. Note the structure: the jackpot dominates the EV despite being nearly unwinnable, which is exactly why jackpots are advertised and payout percentages are not. Buying a ticket buys entertainment and a fantasy; priced as an investment, it fails immediately.
A school raffle sells 400 tickets at $5 each for a single $1,200 prize. I bought 5 tickets. Was that a good deal, and what were my chances?

Expected value per ticket: the prize pool returning to players is $1,200 spread over 400 tickets, so each ticket is worth $3.00 in expectation. You paid $5 for $3.00 of expected value — as a gamble it's poor, keeping only 60 cents per dollar.

Your chance of winning with 5 of 400 tickets is 5/400 = 1.25% — about 1 in 80.

Context matters though: the raffle takes in 400 x $5 = $2,000, pays $1,200, and keeps $800 for the school. The honest framing is that each ticket is a $3 donation bundled with a $2 lottery ticket. If you'd donate anyway, the raffle is a fine way to do it; if you bought purely to profit, the arithmetic says no.
Parking decision: the garage costs $12 a day. Street parking is free, but enforcement is patchy — I'd guess an 18% chance of a $75 ticket on any given day. Which is cheaper in the long run?

Expected daily cost of the street: 0.18 x $75 = $13.50. The garage is a flat $12. On pure expectation, the garage wins by $1.50 a day — about $33 a month for a daily commuter.

But watch the sensitivity: the whole answer hangs on the enforcement probability. If your true ticket chance is 10%, the street's expected cost drops to $7.50 and the street wins comfortably. The break-even probability is 12/75 = 16%.

So the decision procedure is: estimate your ticket rate from experience (tickets received / days parked), compare with 16%, and choose. Expected value doesn't remove judgment — it tells you exactly which judgment matters.
My car insurance offers $1,900/year with a $500 deductible, or $1,520/year with a $2,000 deductible. I estimate a 9% chance of an at-fault claim in a year. Which should I pick?

The high-deductible plan saves $380 a year in premium, guaranteed. Its cost: if you do claim, you pay $1500 more out of pocket. Expected extra cost: 0.09 x $1500 = $135 per year.

Net expected advantage of the high deductible: $380 - $135 = $245 per year. The break-even claim probability is 380/1500 = 25.3% — you'd need to claim more often than about one year in four before the low deductible wins on expectation.

The condition: this logic only works if you can actually absorb a $2,000 surprise bill. Expected value assumes you can ride out the bad outcome; if a $2,000 hit would go on a credit card at 25% APR, the calculus changes and the low deductible can be the right buy. EV first, liquidity second, then decide.
A climbing gym charges $16 per visit or $260 for a season pass. I went 12 times last season. Pass or pay per visit?

Break-even visits: $260 / $16 = 16.2 — you need 17 visits before the pass pays off. At last season's 12 visits, the pass would have cost you $21.67 per visit, worse than the $16 walk-in price, and you'd have overpaid by $68.

The judgment call is whether owning the pass changes your behaviour — for some people it genuinely does, and going 18 times because the marginal visit feels free is a real effect, not a fallacy. But count it honestly: only buy the pass if you expect the behaviour change, not last season's pattern, to clear 16 visits. Gyms price passes precisely because most buyers overestimate their future attendance.

A buffet costs $26. When I order from a menu at this place I usually get an entree and a drink for about $23, though on hungry days I add an appetizer and dessert and hit $31. Is the buffet a good deal for me?

Put probabilities on your own behaviour. Say 60% of visits you'd order the $23 meal and 40% the $31 spread. Your expected menu spend is 0.6 x $23 + 0.4 x $31 = $26.20 — almost exactly the buffet price. On pure dollars it's a wash.

So the decision rides on second-order effects the EV can't see: the buffet removes the option value of choosing per-visit (some days you'd rather spend $14 on a light lunch, and the buffet charges you $26 anyway), it tempts you to eat past enjoyment to 'win', and it wins when your appetite is unpredictable. Expected value frames the question — it correctly tells you the price is fair for your average appetite — but the variance of your appetite, not the mean, is where the buffet makes or loses money on you.
A sportsbook gives me a '$50 free bet' token. If I bet it on an even-money shot and win, I get $50 profit but not the $50 stake back. What is the token really worth?

Expected value: you win with probability about 1/2 and collect $50; you lose and collect $0 — and the stake was never yours to keep. EV = 0.5 x $50 = $25. The '$50 free bet' is worth about $25 before you place it.

Refinement: an even-money line at a bookmaker isn't a true coin flip — the odds embed the book's margin, so your pick's true win probability is closer to 48%, making the token worth about $24.

The general principle transfers: any promotional credit that pays out winnings but not stake is worth roughly half its face value at even odds, and less on favourites (small payouts) — counterintuitively, free bets return more expected value on longshots, because the missing stake matters less when the payout is large. Promotions are priced by people who have done this arithmetic; do it too.

A $5 scratch card has this prize structure: $500 with probability 1/2,000; $50 with probability 1/200; $10 with probability 1/20; $5 (your money back) with probability 1/10; otherwise nothing. Compute the expected value of one card and the game's payout percentage.

Expected value = sum over prizes of (prize x probability):

$500 tier: 500 x 1/2000 = $0.25
$50 tier: 50 x 1/200 = $0.25
$10 tier: 10 x 1/20 = $0.50
$5 tier: 5 x 1/10 = $0.50

Total EV = $1.50 on a $5 card — a payout percentage of 30%. The operator keeps 70 cents of every dollar, before printing and retail costs.

Note the design: the $5 'money back' tier is the most common prize and feels like not losing, but it returns exactly your stake — it contributes $0.50 of EV while generating most of the game's 'I won something' moments. Prize structures are engineered around that feeling; the EV table is the antidote.

A warehouse store sells a 30-roll pack of paper towels for $24. My local shop sells single rolls at $1.10. We use about 18 rolls a year. There's maybe a 20% chance we'll move house in 10 months and I'd leave the leftover rolls behind. Is the bulk pack actually cheaper?

Naive comparison: the pack costs $0.80 per roll vs $1.10 single — but the pack holds 30 rolls and you use 18 a year, so it lasts about 20 months, which exposes you to the move.

If you move at month 10, you'll have used about 15 rolls and abandon 15 rolls worth 15 x $0.80 = $12. Expected loss: 0.20 x $12 = $2.40. Effective expected cost of the pack: $24 + $2.40 = $26.40 for an expected 27 usable rolls — about $0.98 per usable roll.

Versus buying singles as needed: 30 rolls x $1.10 = $33 with zero waste risk. The bulk pack still wins on expectation, but the margin shrank from a headline 27% saving to roughly 20% — and if your move probability were 50%, it would flip. Bulk discounts are bets on your own stability; price them that way.
Phone insurance costs $13/month. It covers a cracked screen: repair is $180 without the plan, or a $29 deductible with it. I estimate a 25% chance of cracking my screen in a year. Run the numbers.

Without the plan, your expected annual cost is just the risk: 0.25 x $180 = $45.

With the plan, you pay $156 in premiums for certain, plus the expected deductible: 0.25 x $29 = $7.25, for an expected total of about $163.

So the plan costs roughly $118 a year more in expectation. That gap is the price of converting a possible $180 shock into a certain $13 monthly drip. For someone whose budget can't absorb surprises, that can be a rational purchase — but recognize what you're buying: cash-flow smoothing, not savings. Also stress-test the assumption: the plan only approaches break-even if your annual crack probability is near 103%, which is true for very few people but genuinely true for some jobs and some toddlers.

Trip insurance costs $110 on a $2,400 trip. If I have to cancel, I lose about 70% of the trip cost in non-refundable bookings. My honest chance of cancelling is around 6%. Is the policy priced fairly?

Expected loss without insurance: 0.06 x (0.70 x $2,400) = 0.06 x $1,680 = $101. The policy costs $110 — almost exactly your expected loss, which makes it close to actuarially fair (real policies usually price above expected loss, so either your cancellation chance is a bit higher than 6% or this policy is competitive).

When a policy is priced near fair, expected value stops deciding and risk tolerance starts: $1,680 is a loss you'd feel, and the insurer pools thousands of travellers so the law of large numbers protects it, not you. Fair-price insurance on a loss that would genuinely sting is a reasonable buy. Where EV does bite is the reverse case — when the premium is three or four times the expected loss, as with most extended warranties, you're overpaying for the smoothing.
I bet $20 on black at roulette every spin. What's my expected result per spin, and over an hour of play at 60 spins an hour?

On an American wheel, 18 of 38 pockets are black, 20 are not (18 red plus 2 green zeros). Per spin: you win $20 with probability 18/38 and lose $20 with probability 20/38. Expected value = 20 x (18/38) - 20 x (20/38) = $-1.05 per spin.

Over 60 spins: 60 x $-1.05 = about $-63 expected loss per hour. You staked $1,200 of total action in that hour, so the house edge is 5.3% of everything you bet.

This is the number casinos are built on: not any single spin (you'll win plenty of individual spins — 47% of them) but the relentless $1.05 toll on every spin, compounding with time. Expected value per bet times number of bets is the whole business model.
A store sells $100 gift cards for $85 during a promotion. I figure there's a 10% chance any given card I buy ends up lost or forgotten. Good deal?

If you would definitely spend $100 at that store anyway, the expected value of what the card returns is 0.90 x $100 = $90 — you paid $85 for an expected $90 of goods, a modest win.

Now the trap: suppose only 80% of the card's face value represents spending you'd actually do at full price there, and the rest is stuff you'd buy only because the card is burning a hole in your pocket. Then the card returns 0.90 x 0.80 x $100 = $72 of genuine value for your $85 — a loss.

This is why breakage (unredeemed cards) and induced spending make gift-card promotions profitable for stores even at a 15% discount. The EV question is never just 'will I redeem it?' but 'would every dollar of it have been spent here anyway?'

A streaming service costs $16/month. Renting a movie digitally costs $5.99. In a typical month I watch either 1 movie (about a quarter of months), 2 movies (half of months), or 4 movies (a quarter of months). Subscribe or rent?

Expected movies per month: 0.25 x 1 + 0.50 x 2 + 0.25 x 4 = 2.25. Expected rental cost: 2.25 x $5.99 = $13.48 a month — less than the $16 subscription.

The subscription only wins if your viewing rises to about 2.7 movies a month on average. Subscriptions sell you the top of your distribution ('some months I watch tons') and charge you for it every month, including the 1-movie months.

Caveat: this counts only movies. If the service also replaces other viewing you'd otherwise pay for, add that to the rental side. The method is the point — price the subscription against your expected usage distribution, not your best month.

A dealer offers a 2-year warranty on a used car for $2,200. A mechanic estimates these repair risks over the next two years: transmission failure 5% costing $3,800; air-conditioning repair 15% costing $900; electronics repair 20% costing $450; minor repairs 25% costing $300. Compute the expected repair cost without the warranty and evaluate the offer.

Expected cost of each risk (probability x cost):

transmission failure: 5% chance x $3,800 = $190
air-conditioning repair: 15% chance x $900 = $135
electronics repair: 20% chance x $450 = $90
minor repairs: 25% chance x $300 = $75

Total expected repair cost: $490 over two years. The warranty costs $2,200 — about 4.5 times the expected losses it covers.

Verdict on the numbers: decline, and self-insure by putting the $2,200 in a repair fund. The important caveat is variance: there is a 5% chance of a $3,800 transmission bill, and expected value treats that the same as a certain $190. If a $3,800 surprise would force high-interest debt, paying for certainty can be defended — but at 4.5x the expected cost, you'd be paying an extreme premium for it. Most buyers at this price are purchasing against a risk they could actually absorb.
Someone in my office spends their lunch breaks entering online sweepstakes — each entry takes about 3 minutes. A typical prize is $10,000 with about 2 million entries. Is this a sensible side hustle?

Expected value per entry: $10,000 / 2,000,000 = $0.005 — half a cent. At 3 minutes per entry, that's 20 entries an hour, so the expected earnings are about $0.10 per hour.

Ten cents an hour is the whole analysis. The reason it feels productive is that the prize is vivid and the probability is invisible — nobody can picture 2 million entries, so the brain quietly substitutes 'someone wins, why not me' for the actual rate.

Expected value has a second use here: pricing your own time. Any activity with a calculable EV per hour can be compared against literally any other use of the hour. Sweepstakes at $0.10/hr lose to nearly everything, including rest.
My coworker says buying two lottery tickets instead of one 'doubles my chances' so it's twice as smart. The jackpot draw has 13,983,816 possible combinations. Respond to the logic.

The arithmetic is true and the conclusion is empty. One ticket wins with probability 1/13,983,816, about 7.15e-08. Two distinct tickets win with probability 2/13,983,816 — yes, exactly double.

But doubling a negligible probability leaves a negligible probability: you'd need to buy about 6,991,908 tickets to reach a 50% chance, and at that point you've spent nearly $14 million (at $1 a ticket) chasing a jackpot that's usually smaller. Relative change ('double!') and absolute change (from 0.0000072% to 0.0000143%) tell opposite stories, and advertisers of everything from lotteries to supplements choose the relative one.

Also note: the second ticket doesn't change your expected value per dollar at all — each ticket loses the same fraction on average. 'Twice as smart' would require the deal to improve, not just the stake to grow.

Flight choice: non-refundable ticket $310, or refundable for $390. If my plans change, rebooking the non-refundable ticket costs about $180 in fees and fare difference. I estimate a 35% chance my plans change. Which ticket?

Expected extra cost of the non-refundable ticket: 0.35 x $180 = $63. The refundable ticket charges you $80 extra for certain. $80 > $63, so on expectation the non-refundable ticket wins by about $17.

The break-even change probability is $80/$180 = 44% — if you think there's more than a 44% chance of changing plans, buy the refundable fare.

Two refinements worth making before deciding: first, 'plans change' losses are capped by the $180 figure only if you'd still take the trip; if a change means abandoning the ticket entirely, the loss is $310 and the break-even drops to 26%. Second, flexibility has option value beyond the fee — a refundable ticket lets you grab a cheaper flight later. Expected value gives you the threshold; your real uncertainty about the 35% should decide which side of it you're on.

A home warranty costs $45/month plus a $75 fee per service visit. My rough annual chances of needing covered repairs: plumber 30% (typical bill $350), an appliance repair 20% ($400), HVAC repair 10% ($600). Evaluate it.

Annual premium: $45 x 12 = $540, paid for certain.

Expected repair bills without the warranty: 0.30 x $350 + 0.20 x $400 + 0.10 x $600 = $245 a year.

With the warranty you still pay service fees: expected number of claims is 0.6 a year, so expected fees are 0.6 x $75 = $45. Your expected total with the warranty is $540 + $45 = $585, versus $245 expected without it — the warranty costs you roughly $340 a year in expectation.

And that comparison is generous to the warranty: it ignores claim denials, depreciation schedules, and the fact that the warranty company chooses the cheapest repair. Home warranties are among the most reliably negative-EV products sold, because the seller's entire margin structure depends on premiums exceeding claims by a wide factor. Self-insuring with a home-repair savings account beats it on the math for anyone who can hold the reserve.
What is the 'rule of 72' and how accurate is it?

Divide 72 by the annual percentage growth rate to get the approximate doubling time in years. At 4% growth, money (or anything else growing steadily) doubles in about 72/4 = 18 years; at 6%, 12 years; at 8%, 9 years; at 12%, 6 years.

Accuracy check at 8%: the rule says 9 years, and the exact figure is ln(2)/ln(1.08) = 9.0 years — very close. At 2% the rule gives 36 years vs an exact 35.0; at 20% it gives 3.6 years vs an exact 3.8. The rule is best in the 4-12% band where most real decisions live.

Why 72 and not the 'natural' 69.3 (which is 100 x ln 2)? Because 72 divides cleanly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 12, and the slight upward fudge compensates for the discrete annual compounding the pure logarithm ignores. It's a mental-math tool: use it to smell-check any growth claim in seconds, then compute exactly if the decision matters.
I have a $3,000 credit card balance at about 25% APR. If I paid nothing at all, how fast would the debt grow?

At 25% APR the rule of 72 gives a doubling time of 72/25, about 2.9 years. So roughly: $3,000 becomes $6,000 in about 3 years, and $12,000 in about 6. Exact compounding at 25% annually gives 3000 x 1.25^6 = $11,444 after six years — slightly ahead of the rule-of-72 sketch because the rule rounds.

Two practical footnotes. First, real cards compound monthly and add late fees and penalty APRs, so the true trajectory is worse than this clean curve. Second, minimum payments are designed to keep you near the top of the curve: a typical minimum of interest plus 1% of the balance means the balance shrinks at a crawl while interest accrues at full speed. The doubling-time framing is the honest way to feel an APR: 25% doesn't mean 'a quarter extra', it means 'twice as much debt every three years'.
Inflation is running at 3% a year. What does that actually do over the length of a career?

At 3% inflation, prices double in about 72/3 = 24 years. A basket of goods costing $100 today costs 100 x 1.03^24 = $203 in 24 years, and about $413 in 48.

Run it backwards for savings: cash sitting in a drawer for 24 years loses half its purchasing power — $10,000 becomes the equivalent of about $4,919 in today's money. And a salary frozen for a decade at 3% inflation is a pay cut of 26% in real terms, even though the number on the payslip never changed.

This is why 'keeping money safe under the mattress' is a slow guaranteed loss, and why long-term comparisons must always be made in inflation-adjusted (real) terms. The growth rate that matters is the one after inflation is subtracted.
A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting from a single cell, how many descendants are there after 12 hours, and why doesn't this go on forever?

Twelve hours is 720 minutes, which is 36 doubling periods. Starting from one cell: 2^36 = 68,719,476,736 cells — about 69 billion.

Sanity check the mass: a bacterium weighs about a picogram (10^-12 g), so 0 billion cells is only about 0 grams of bacteria. The count sounds astronomical while the physical amount is a smear — a good reminder that exponential counts and physical scale are different things.

Why it stops: exponential growth assumes unlimited food, space, and waste removal. In a real culture the bacteria exhaust nutrients and poison themselves with waste, and growth bends into the logistic S-curve — flat at the environment's carrying capacity. Every real exponential is the early chapter of an S-curve; the skill is asking what the limiting resource is and when it binds.
Is it true that if you could fold a piece of paper 42 times, it would reach the Moon?

The arithmetic is real. A sheet of paper is about 0.1 mm thick. Each fold doubles the thickness, so after 42 folds: 0.0001 m x 2^42 = 439,804,651 metres — about 439,805 km. The Moon is about 384,400 km away, so yes, the folded stack would overshoot it.

The intermediate steps show why intuition fails: after just 10 folds the stack is 10 cm thick — a hand's width. After 20 folds, 0 km. After 30, 107 km. Almost everything happens in the last few doublings.

The catch is physical, not mathematical: paper can't actually be folded more than about 7-12 times because the fold radius and paper loss grow exponentially too. Treat the claim as a demonstration of doubling, not an engineering plan — exponentials in textbooks assume the process never hits a constraint, and reality always supplies one.

An algae bloom doubles its coverage of a reservoir every day. On day 40 it covers the whole surface. A ranger says 'on day 33 it was barely 1% — nobody worried.' Was the bloom really that small a week before the reservoir was fully covered?

Work backwards from full coverage. Day 40: 100%. Day 39: 50%. Day 38: 25%. Day 37: 12.5%. Day 36: about 6%. Day 35: about 3%. Day 34: about 1.6%. Day 33: 2^(33-40) = 1/128, about 0.8%.

So yes, the ranger is right about the observation and the worry was still justified: with daily doubling, the bloom spends most of its life looking negligible and then covers the last 99% in a single week. Going from 1% to 100% takes fewer than 7 doublings.

This is the general trap of exponential processes — epidemics, debt, viral content, invasive species. By the time the problem looks big, you are one or two doubling periods from it being unmanageable. The time to act on an exponential is when it looks trivially small, which is precisely when action feels hardest to justify.
An account has 2,000 followers and is growing 7% per week. How long until it doubles, and where is it in six months if the rate holds?

Doubling time: the rule of 72 gives 72/7, about 10 weeks; the exact figure is ln(2)/ln(1.07) = 10.2 weeks.

Six months is 26 weeks of compounding: 2,000 x 1.07^26 = about 11,615 followers. Note what happened: two and a half doublings turned 2,000 into nearly 5.8x as many — growth of 'just 7% a week' is ferocious when sustained.

The professional caveat: weekly percentage growth almost never holds for 26 straight weeks, because audiences saturate and the easy followers arrive first. Quote the projection as 'if the current rate persisted' and re-fit the rate monthly. An exponential model is a local description, not a prophecy — but for the next few weeks it beats a linear guess, which would predict only 2,000 + 26 x 140 = 5,640 and badly undershoot.

You save $250 a month into an investment earning 7% a year, compounded monthly. Compute the value after 30 years and after 40 years, and how much of each total is your own contributions versus growth.

Monthly rate r = 0.07/12 = 0.00583. The future value of a monthly payment stream is FV = 250 x ((1 + r)^n - 1) / r.

After 30 years (n = 360): FV = about $304,993. Your contributions: 250 x 360 = $90,000. Growth contributed the other $214,993 — about 70% of the final pile.

After 40 years (n = 480): FV = about $656,203. Contributions: $120,000. Growth: $536,203, about 82% of the total.

The lesson is in the difference: the extra decade adds only $30,000 of contributions but about $351,211 of final value. Compounding rewards time in the market superlinearly because in the later years the accumulated growth itself is generating most of the new growth. Starting ten years earlier beats saving considerably more per month for most people — run the comparison before assuming you can 'catch up later'.
A scheme promises returns if I recruit 5 people, each of whom recruits 5 more, and so on. Why do people say these always collapse? Show me with numbers.

Count the levels. Level 1: you. Level 2: 5 recruits. Level 3: 25. Each level multiplies by 5, so level k needs 5^(k-1) fresh people. By level 12 the scheme needs 48,828,125 new recruits in that level alone, and the total membership is already about 305 million.

Level 13 needs 1.2 billion new people in a single level — a substantial fraction of everyone on Earth. Level 15 would need 6 billion, several times the human population. The scheme doesn't collapse because of fraud investigations or bad luck; it collapses arithmetically, because exponential recruitment exhausts any finite population within a dozen or so levels.

And the geometry decides who loses: in any such scheme, the bottom levels — which must be the vast majority of all members, since each level is 5x the one above — are the ones who paid in and cannot recruit. Roughly 80%+ of everyone who ever joins is in the final two levels. When someone shows you a recruitment tree, ask which level you'd be on.
An outbreak starts with 40 known cases and is doubling every 3.5 days. Roughly how many cases after 5 weeks if nothing changes?

Five weeks is 35 days, which is 35 / 3.5 = 10 doubling periods. Cases: 40 x 2^10 = 40 x 1,024 = 40,960.

Notice the rhythm of the growth: after 2 weeks (4 doublings) there are only 640 cases — looks containable. After 3.5 weeks, 5,120. The final doubling alone adds 20,480 cases, more than the entire history of the outbreak to that point. In exponential growth, the last doubling always contributes half of everything.

'If nothing changes' is doing heavy lifting: real outbreaks bend the curve as behaviour changes, immunity accumulates, and interventions bite. The exponential projection isn't a prediction — it's the cost of delay, expressed as a number. Each 3.5 days of delay at this stage costs a factor of two.
My photo library has 25,000 photos and grows about 18% a year. When does it double, and how big is it in 10 years?

Doubling time: ln(2)/ln(1.18) = 4.2 years (the rule of 72 gives 72/18 = 4 years, close enough for planning).

In 10 years at 18% growth: 25,000 x 1.18^10 = about 130,846 photos — more than a fivefold increase, because 10 years is nearly two and a half doublings.

Translate to storage to make it actionable: at about 4 MB a photo, that's roughly 100 GB today becoming about 525 GB in a decade. The planning lesson generalises: any quantity growing at a steady percentage — data, debt, subscribers, costs — should be managed on its doubling clock, not its current size. 'It's only 100 GB' is a statement about today; the doubling time is the statement about your future.

In the classic chessboard problem, one grain of rice is placed on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time. A rice grain weighs about 25 mg. Compute: grains on square 20, grains on square 30, the total for all 64 squares, and the total mass. Compare the mass with world rice production of roughly 500 million tonnes per year.

Square n holds 2^(n-1) grains.

Square 20: 2^19 = 524,288 grains (about half a million).
Square 30: 2^29 = 536,870,912 grains (over half a billion — the count grows by a factor of about 1,000 every 10 squares).
Total for 64 squares: 2^64 - 1 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains, about 1.8 x 10^19.

Mass: 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 x 25 mg = about 4.61e+14 kg, i.e. 461169 billion tonnes. World production is about 5 x 10^11 kg per year, so the chessboard total equals roughly 922 years of global rice harvests.

The instructive feature is where the mass sits: the 64th square alone holds half the grand total, and squares 33-64 hold essentially everything. Exponentials concentrate their impact at the end of the sequence, which is why extrapolating from the tame early squares ('square 10 is only 512 grains') is the classic blunder.
Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours in the body. I drink a coffee with 200 mg at noon. How much is still in my system at 6 pm, at midnight, and at noon the next day?

Half-life decay: amount = 200 x 2^(-t/5).

At 6 pm (t = 6): 200 x 2^(-1.2) = about 87 mg — more than a small coffee's worth still active, which surprises people.
At midnight (t = 12): 200 x 2^(-2.4) = about 38 mg.
At noon next day (t = 24): 200 x 2^(-4.8) = about 7 mg — nearly gone, but not zero.

Half-life is exponential growth run in reverse, and the same intuition traps apply: the amount never quite reaches zero, the early hours remove far more than the later ones, and 'it's been hours, it must be out of my system' is wrong by a factor you can compute. It also explains stacking: a second coffee at 4 pm doesn't replace the first, it adds to the roughly {200*2**(-4/5):.0f} mg still circulating from it.
I earn $60,000. My raises are 2% a year but inflation is 3.5% a year. My manager says my pay has gone up every year for ten years. Has it?

Nominally, yes: $60,000 x 1.02^10 = $73,140 after ten years — a bigger number every single year.

In purchasing power, no. Prices over the same decade rose by a factor of 1.035^10 = 1.41. Divide your nominal pay by that: $73,140 / 1.41 = $51,850 in today's money. Your salary now buys 86% of what it bought ten years ago — a real pay cut of about 14%.

The rule: real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation (2% - 3.5% = -1.5% a year), and a decade of -1.5% compounds to about -14%. Any long-horizon money comparison — salaries, savings, house prices, 'record' box office — that isn't inflation-adjusted is quietly lying in the same direction, flattering whoever reports the nominal number.
Which grows more: money at 9% a year for 8 years, or at 4.5% a year for 16 years?

Compute both. At 9% for 8 years: 1.09^8 = 1.993 — your money roughly doubles (the rule of 72 says 72/9 = 8 years per doubling, exactly this case).

At 4.5% for 16 years: 1.045^16 = 2.022 — also roughly a doubling, which the rule of 72 predicts too: 72/4.5 = 16 years per doubling.

The slower rate over double the time edges it out slightly (2.022 vs 1.993) because compounding is convex: growth on growth keeps accelerating. The deeper point is that rate and time trade against each other through the doubling clock — halving the rate doesn't halve the outcome if you double the horizon. This is why 'when do you start?' usually matters more than 'which fund is 1% better?' in long-term saving.
How different are a million, a billion, and a trillion seconds, really?

Convert each to human time. A million seconds: 1,000,000 / 86,400 = about 11.6 days — a week and a half. A billion seconds: about 32 years — most of an adult lifetime. A trillion seconds: about 31,688 years — longer than recorded history several times over; you'd have to start before the invention of agriculture.

Each step up is a factor of 1,000, but the felt difference is far bigger than 'three more zeros' suggests, because the units themselves change character: days, then a lifespan, then geological-feeling time. This is the single most useful calibration in public life. When a budget, a debt, or a dataset is quoted in billions versus trillions, translate to a rate or a per-person figure before reacting — raw counts at this scale carry almost no intuition at all.
The national debt is about $34 trillion and the US population is about 335 million. What is that per person, and is per-person the right way to think about it?

The division: $34 x 10^12 / 335 x 10^6 = about $101,493 per person. Per household (about 131 million households): about $259,542.

Per-person conversion is the right first move — it turns an ungraspable count into a graspable one — but it has limits worth naming. The debt isn't owed by individuals in equal shares, it isn't all due at once, and much of it is held by the public and institutions as assets on the other side of the ledger. A per-person figure answers 'how big is this, in units I understand?' It does not answer 'what would it cost to pay off?' or 'is this sustainable?' — those depend on interest rates versus growth rates, not on the raw total.

Use per-capita translation for scale, then switch tools for the policy question. Confusing the two is how both 'the debt is nothing' and 'the debt is a household credit card' arguments go wrong.

The Richter/moment magnitude scale is logarithmic: each whole step up multiplies ground-motion amplitude by 10 and energy release by about 31.6 (10^1.5). A magnitude 5 quake is the reference (energy E). Express the amplitude and energy of magnitude 6, 7, and 8 relative to magnitude 5, and comment on the headline 'a magnitude 8 is only a bit bigger than a 7'.

Relative to magnitude 5 (amplitude 1, energy E):

Magnitude 6: amplitude x10, energy x32 (10^1.5 = 31.6).
Magnitude 7: amplitude x100, energy x1,000 (10^3).
Magnitude 8: amplitude x1,000, energy x31,623 (10^4.5 = 31,623).

So a magnitude 8 releases about 31.6 times the energy of a magnitude 7, and about 31,600 times a magnitude 5. 'Only one point higher' on a log scale is not a small difference — the scale was designed to compress an enormous physical range into single digits, and it compresses the differences too.

The general skill: whenever a quantity is reported on a logarithmic scale (earthquakes, decibels, pH, stellar magnitude), differences are ratios. A 1-point gap always means the same multiple, no matter where on the scale it sits.
A conversation is about 60 decibels and a nearby siren is about 120 decibels. The numbers differ by 60 — how much more intense is the siren, actually?

Decibels are logarithmic: every 10 dB multiplies sound intensity by 10. A 60 dB gap is six steps of 10, so the intensity ratio is 10^6 — the siren's sound is about 1,000,000.0 times as intense as the conversation.

Perceived loudness follows a different rule: roughly, every 10 dB sounds about twice as loud. Six steps of doubling gives 2^6 = 64.0 — the siren sounds on the order of 64 times louder, not a million times.

Both numbers are correct; they measure different things (physical intensity versus perception). This is why dB figures mislead casually: 'twice the decibels' (60 to 120) sounds like 'twice as much', while the physics moved by six orders of magnitude and perception by less than two. When a scale is logarithmic, always ask: difference in what — the log value, the underlying quantity, or the perceived effect?
Vinegar is about pH 3 and coffee is about pH 5. A friend says vinegar is 'a bit more acidic, two points more'. Correct them.

pH is a logarithmic scale of hydrogen-ion concentration: each point down multiplies acidity by 10. Two points means 10^2 = 100 — vinegar is about 100 times as acidic as coffee, not 'a bit' more.

Extend it: stomach acid at about pH 2 is 1,000 times as acidic as coffee, and pure water at pH 7 is 10,000 times less acidic than vinegar. The whole everyday range from stomach acid to soap spans about ten orders of magnitude, compressed into the friendly little numbers 2 through 10ish.

Log scales exist precisely because the underlying quantity ranges too widely for a linear scale to be usable. The price is that arithmetic on the labels ('two points more') silently becomes multiplication on the reality. Whenever you see pH, decibels, or magnitudes, translate differences into ratios before drawing any conclusion.
If you stacked a million pennies, how tall would the stack be? And what would it be worth?

A US penny is 1.52 mm thick. A million of them: 1,000,000 x 1.52 mm = 1,520 metres — about 1.5 km tall, or roughly 4.6 Eiffel Towers stacked (at 330 m each).

The value is anticlimactic: a million pennies is $10,000. A kilometre-and-a-half tower of money that buys a used car.

That's the charm of order-of-magnitude thinking: it exposes where intuition misfires. 'A million' sounds like wealth and like an unimaginable count; converted to height it's a modest skyscraper-stack, converted to dollars it's five figures. Big round numbers have no fixed meaning until you attach a unit and a conversion.
How long would it take to walk around the Earth at the equator, walking 40 km a day?

Earth's equatorial circumference is about 40,075 km. At 40 km a day: 40,075 / 40 = about 1,002 days — roughly 2.7 years of walking every single day.

Sanity check the pace: 40 km a day at a typical 5 km/h walking speed is 8 hours of walking daily — a full working day, sustained for nearly three years. Real circumnavigations on foot take 4-7 years once rest, weather, borders, and oceans (which rather interrupt a walk) are included.

The estimate's job isn't precision; it's to sort the answer into the right mental bucket — 'a season' versus 'years' versus 'a lifetime'. Many planning errors are bucket errors, and a 60-second division like this prevents them.
Could the entire human population stand together in one place? How much area would 8.1 billion people need just to stand?

Give each standing person a tight but plausible 0.2 square metres (about 45 cm by 45 cm — crowd density, not comfort). Total: 8.1 x 10^9 x 0.2 = 1,620 square kilometres.

That's roughly the size of Greater London (about 1,570 sq km) — the entire species, standing shoulder to shoulder, fits in one metropolitan area with room to spare. Even at a comfortable 1 square metre each, it's 8,100 sq km, smaller than many countries' single national parks.

The point isn't the party trick. Population anxiety often runs on imagery of physical crowding, but the binding constraints are never standing room — they're food, water, energy, and waste flows, which scale with consumption, not body area. Order-of-magnitude checks tell you which resource actually binds; argue about that one.
My new drive is 2 TB. Photos are about 4 MB each and 4K video runs about 400 MB per minute. How much of each fits?

Work in megabytes: 2 TB is about 2,000,000 MB. Photos: 2,000,000 / 4 = 500,000 photos. Video: 2,000,000 / 400 = 5,000 minutes = about 83 hours.

The comparison is the lesson: one minute of 4K video costs the storage of 100 photos. Media types differ by orders of magnitude in appetite, so 'how big is the drive?' has no answer until you specify the mix — a drive that is effectively infinite for documents (40 million text files at 50 KB) is a weekend of video.

Practical corollary: when a storage or bandwidth estimate is off by 100x, the cause is almost always a unit slip (MB vs GB, bits vs bytes) — internet speeds are quoted in megabits, files in megabytes, a factor of 8 that has embarrassed many estimates. Write the units in every line of the calculation.
I counted 9 seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder. How far away was the strike?

Light arrives essentially instantly; sound travels at about 343 m/s. Distance = 343 x 9 = 3,087 metres — about 3 km.

That's the origin of the folk rule 'count the seconds and divide by three to get kilometres' (or divide by five for miles). The rule works because 343 m/s is close to 1 km per 3 seconds.

It's also a tidy example of an order-of-magnitude instrument built into everyday life: your ears plus counting give a range estimate good to maybe 20%, which is all you need for the actual decision (keep swimming or get out of the pool). Not every measurement needs a lab; it needs precision matched to the decision it feeds.
Estimate the number of grains of sand in a 10-litre bucket.

A typical sand grain is about 0.5 mm across. As a sphere of radius 0.025 cm, its volume is 4/3 pi r^3 = about 6.5e-05 cubic centimetres. The bucket holds 10 litres = 10,000 cubic centimetres, and poured grains pack at about 60% efficiency, so the grains occupy 6,000 cubic centimetres of actual sand.

Divide: 6,000 / 6.5e-05 = about 9.2e+07 — roughly a hundred million grains in a bucket.

Sensitivity check: if the grains are coarse (1 mm), each has 8x the volume and the count drops to about 1e+07; if fine (0.25 mm), it rises 8-fold to near 7e+08. The estimate is honest as 'order 10^8' — and now the famous 'grains of sand on all beaches' figure of around 10^18-10^19 becomes checkable rather than mystical: it's about 10^10-10^11 bucketfuls, spread over the world's coastlines.
Give me a comparison that makes the speed of light feel concrete versus a passenger jet.

Earth's circumference is about 40,075 km. Light at 300,000 km/s circles it 300,000 / 40,075 = about 7.5 times per second. A jet at 900 km/h needs 40,075 / 900 = about 45 hours for one loop — nearly two days.

In one second, the jet covers 250 metres; light covers 300,000 km. The ratio of the speeds is about 1e+06 — light is roughly a million times faster.

Concretely: a phone call routed via a geostationary satellite travels up 36,000 km and back down, twice — about 144,000 km — taking roughly half a second, which is why satellite calls have that perceptible lag while a fibre call across an ocean (light in glass, ~200,000 km/s) feels instant. At everyday scales light is effectively infinite in speed; at planetary scales its finiteness becomes an engineering budget. Order-of-magnitude fluency is knowing which regime you're in.

Biologists studying a lake's fish population catch and tag 240 fish, then release them. A week later they catch 150 fish, of which 18 carry tags. Estimate the total fish population, state the key assumption, and give one reason the estimate could be biased.

Method: capture-recapture. If the tagged fish have mixed evenly into the population, the fraction tagged in the second catch should equal the fraction tagged in the whole lake.

18/150 = 12% of the second catch is tagged. So tagged fish (240) should be about 12% of the population: N = 240 / 0.12 = 2,000 fish. Equivalently, N = (240 x 150) / 18 = 2,000.

Key assumption: the second catch is a representative sample — tagged and untagged fish are equally catchable and fully mixed.

Bias risk (any one of several): if tagged fish become trap-shy (or trap-happy, having learned where food is), the recapture rate misleads; if tagging harmed some fish, the tagged pool shrank; if the lake isn't closed (fish entering or leaving), the population changed between visits. The estimate is only as good as the mixing assumption, which is why biologists repeat the sampling and compare.
We let 20 customers taste-test our old recipe against a new one, blind. 14 preferred the new one. The chef says this proves customers prefer it. How strong is this evidence, really?

Weaker than it feels. If customers truly had no preference, each taster is a coin flip, and the chance of 14 or more out of 20 landing on the new recipe by luck alone is the binomial tail: sum of C(20,k) for k = 14..20, divided by 2^20 = 5.8%.

So a 6%-ish event — unusual but not rare; run this test on 17 unchanged recipes and you'd expect one result this lopsided by chance. Conventionally, evidence this strong is 'suggestive, worth a bigger test', not proof.

How much bigger? To reliably detect a true 60/40 preference you'd need on the order of 200 tasters. The intuition to build: with n = 20, the margin of error on a proportion is roughly plus or minus 1/sqrt(20), about 22 points — 14/20 = 70% is consistent with a true preference anywhere from 'coin flip' to 'overwhelming'. Small samples can only detect enormous effects; if the effect might be modest, budget the sample for it.
I asked 12 friends whether they prefer my app's new design, and all 12 said yes. Can I tell my boss support is basically unanimous?

You can tell your boss 12 friends said yes. The inference to 'basically unanimous' fails twice over.

First, pure sampling math: if the true approval rate among users were p, the chance of drawing 12 approvals in a row is p^12. Setting p^12 = 0.05 and solving, p = 0.78 — so even with a unanimous sample of 12, a true approval rate as low as about 78% would still produce your result 5% of the time. The quick 'rule of three' version: with zero dissenters in n tries, dissent could still be as high as about 3/n = 25%.

Second, and worse: your friends are not a random sample of users. They're selected for knowing you, liking you, and sharing your taste — a biased frame that no sample size fixes. Unanimity in a tiny, friendly sample is close to no information about the user base. Report it as a smoke test ('nobody hated it'), not a measurement.

Cafe A has a 4.9-star average from 7 reviews. Cafe B has 4.6 stars from 1,240 reviews. A ranking site wants a fairer comparison and uses this adjustment: blend each cafe's average with the platform-wide average of 4.3 stars, giving the platform average a weight of 50 phantom reviews. Compute both adjusted scores and say which cafe should rank first.

Cafe A: (7 x 4.9 + 50 x 4.3) / (7 + 50) = (34.3 + 215) / 57 = 4.37.
Cafe B: (1240 x 4.6 + 50 x 4.3) / (1240 + 50) = (5704 + 215) / 1290 = 4.59.

Cafe B ranks first, 4.59 vs 4.37 — the ranking flips. Cafe A's gaudy 4.9 rests on seven opinions and gets pulled most of the way toward the platform mean; Cafe B's 4.6 rests on 1,240 opinions and barely moves.

This is shrinkage, the standard cure for small-sample extremes: distrust averages built on little data by blending them toward the overall average in proportion to their thinness. It explains why 'sort by rating' on any marketplace is meaningless without it — the top of an unadjusted list is always dominated by tiny samples that got lucky. When you see a perfect score, ask for the denominator before anything else.
You roll a die 60 times to check whether it's fair. Six comes up 16 times. Expected count for a fair die, the standard deviation of that count, and a verdict, please.

Expected count: 60 x 1/6 = 10 sixes.
Standard deviation of the count: sqrt(n p (1-p)) = sqrt(60 x 1/6 x 5/6) = 2.9.
Observed: 16, which is (16 - 10) / 2.9 = 2.1 standard deviations above expectation.

A result 2 standard deviations out happens by chance roughly 2-4% of the time for a given face — but you would have been equally suspicious of any face landing at 16, and with six faces the chance that at least one looks this lopsided is much higher, on the order of 15-20%. Verdict: mildly suspicious, nowhere near proof. The fix is more data: at 600 rolls the standard deviation grows only to 9 while a genuinely biased die's excess grows tenfold, so signal outruns noise as sqrt(n) — that's the engine under all sample-size reasoning.
A jar holds 620 jellybeans. You sample 5 handfuls of 20 beans each and count the red ones: 4, 7, 5, 6, 8. Estimate the number of red beans in the jar, with an uncertainty range.

Pooled sample: 30 red out of 100 beans, a proportion of 30%.
Point estimate: 30% x 620 = about 186 red beans.
Uncertainty: the standard error of a proportion is sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = sqrt(0.30 x 0.70 / 100) = 4.6 percentage points. Two standard errors is about 9 points, so the red share is plausibly 21% to 39%, i.e. roughly 129 to 243 red beans.

Two craft notes. First, pooling the five handfuls (100 beans) is what earns the tighter range — each handful alone would carry a standard error of about 10 points. Second, the handfuls must be genuinely mixed draws: if red beans settle to the bottom, handfuls from the top are a biased sample and no amount of pooling repairs it. Precision comes from n; accuracy comes from the sampling method.

A factory inspects 80 randomly chosen units from a production lot of 10,000 and finds zero defects. The manager concludes the lot is defect-free. Quantify what the inspection actually establishes, using the rule of three.

Zero events in a sample does not mean zero risk; it bounds the risk. The rule of three: if you observe 0 events in n trials, the 95% upper confidence bound on the true rate is about 3/n. Here, 3/80 = 3.75%.

So the inspection is consistent with a true defect rate anywhere from 0% up to about 3.8%. At that upper bound, the lot of 10,000 could contain roughly 375 defective units — hardly 'defect-free'.

Why 3? If the true rate were p, seeing zero defects in 80 draws has probability (1-p)^80; setting that to 0.05 and solving gives p = 0.037, and ln(20) is about 3, hence the shortcut. The decision use: work backwards from the rate you must rule out. To certify a defect rate below 0.1% with zero observed defects, you'd need to inspect about 3/0.001 = 3,000 units. Sample size is chosen by the claim you want to defend, not by convenience.
Our poll of 600 voters has a margin of error of about plus or minus 4 points. The campaign wants plus or minus 2 points. How many voters do we need to interview?

Margin of error shrinks with the square root of the sample size, not in proportion to it. Halving the margin requires four times the sample: 600 x 4 = 2,400 voters.

Check with the standard formula: margin is roughly 1/sqrt(n) at the worst case (a 50/50 split). 1/sqrt(600) = 4.1 points; 1/sqrt(2400) = 2.0 points. Matches.

This square-root law is the economics of all measurement: the first few hundred respondents buy you most of the available precision, and each further halving of error costs 4x the previous total budget. It's why national polls cluster around 1,000 respondents (plus or minus about 3 points) — beyond that, extra precision costs more than it's worth for a headline number. And a warning that pairs with it: quadrupling n does nothing for bias. A bigger sample of the wrong people is just a more precise wrong answer.
I flipped a fair coin 100 times and got a run of 6 heads in a row at one point. That can't be chance, can it? The odds of 6 heads in a row are only 1 in 64.

It can, and it usually is. The 1-in-64 figure is the probability that one specific set of 6 flips — say flips 40 through 45 — are all heads. But your 100 flips contain 95 overlapping windows of 6 flips, each with its 1/64 shot.

Expected number of 6-head runs somewhere in 100 flips: about 95/64 = 1.5. Treating occurrences as roughly Poisson, the probability of at least one such run is about 1 - e^(-1.5) = 77%.

So in a hundred flips, a run of six heads (or six tails) is not an anomaly — it's the typical outcome, and its absence would be the surprise. This is the multiple-windows fallacy, and it's everywhere: a 'one-in-a-million' coincidence happens to each person regularly because a life contains millions of windows for coincidences to occur in. Always ask how many chances the surprising event had to happen.
My home blood pressure readings jump around — the standard deviation of a single reading is about 9 mmHg. My doctor averages several readings. How much does averaging actually help?

Averaging n independent readings divides the standard deviation by sqrt(n). One reading: sd 9 mmHg. Average of 4: 9/2 = 4.5 mmHg. Average of 9: 9/3 = 3 mmHg.

To get the noise down to 2 mmHg you'd need n = (9/2)^2 = 20 readings — the square-root law makes extreme precision expensive, which is why doctors settle for averaging 2-3 readings per visit across several visits.

One caveat that matters more than the arithmetic: averaging only cancels random error. If your cuff is the wrong size or you always measure right after climbing stairs, every reading shares the same systematic error and the average is precisely wrong. Random noise yields to repetition; bias yields only to fixing the method. Knowing which kind of error you have decides whether 'take more readings' is the cure or a waste of time.
To estimate the average height of all 900 students at a school, a researcher measures all 25 kids in one first-grade classroom and reports a tight margin of error. What's wrong?

The sample size arithmetic is fine and the sample is useless. Those 25 children share the trait that matters most for height: they're all about six years old. The estimate will be a very precise measurement of first-graders' height and a badly biased estimate of the school's.

This is cluster sampling done wrong. Measuring a whole cluster (one classroom) is efficient, but a single cluster inherits all of that cluster's peculiarities — here, age; in other studies, one neighbourhood, one clinic, one shift at a factory. The reported margin of error only reflects variation within the sample, and it says nothing about the variation between clusters, which is where the real error lives.

The fix isn't necessarily a bigger sample — 25 students drawn randomly across all grades would beat 250 drawn from one classroom. Representativeness is a property of how the sample was drawn, not how large it is. Whenever you see an impressively precise estimate, ask 'a precise measurement of whom?' before believing it describes anyone else.

A pilot study of a new treatment reports that 7 of 8 patients improved, and the press release says the treatment 'works for 87.5% of patients'. Using a Wilson score interval (z = 1.96), compute a 95% confidence interval for the true improvement rate and assess the claim.

Sample proportion: 7/8 = 0.875, n = 8.

Wilson interval: denominator 1 + z^2/n = 1.480; centre = (0.875 + z^2/2n) / 1.480 = 0.753; half-width = 0.224.
95% CI: (0.53, 0.98) — roughly 53% to 98%.

So the data are consistent with a treatment that helps barely half of patients, and also with one that helps nearly all. '87.5%' is the point estimate wearing a suit of false precision: with n = 8, each patient is worth 12.5 percentage points, and the honest headline is 'small pilot, promising, true rate unknown within a 45-point range'.

This is the general state of pilot studies: they exist to check feasibility and safety and to size the real trial, not to estimate effects. Any percentage quoted from a single-digit denominator should be read as an anecdote with arithmetic on top.

A cafe's daily revenue averages $1,200 with a standard deviation of $150 from day to day. The owner compares one week before a menu change with one week after and finds average daily revenue is $60 higher after. She credits the new menu. Assess, using the standard error of a 7-day mean.

Standard error of a 7-day mean: 150 / sqrt(7) = $57. A single week's average naturally wanders by about $57 around the true mean, and the difference between two independent weeks wanders by about sqrt(2) x $57 = $80.

The observed difference is $60 — well inside one standard error of the difference ($80). Ordinary week-to-week luck explains it completely; the menu change may have helped, hurt, or done nothing, and this comparison cannot tell.

How long would she need? To resolve a $60/day effect against $150 daily noise with reasonable confidence takes on the order of (2 x 150/60)^2, roughly 25 days per side — about a month before and after, not a week. Small samples plus noisy daily data is the standard recipe for crediting interventions with weather. Restaurants, retailers, and websites all run this experiment badly every week.
How many people do you need to survey to estimate a proportion within plus or minus 3 percentage points with 95% confidence?

Use the worst case, p = 0.5, which maximises variance: n = z^2 p(1-p) / E^2 = 1.96^2 x 0.25 / 0.03^2 = 1,067. So about 1,068 respondents.

That's why you keep seeing polls of 'about 1,000 people' — ±3 points is the industry's default precision, and this formula is where the number comes from. Note what the formula doesn't contain: the size of the population. Surveying a city of 100,000 and a country of 300 million need essentially the same n for the same precision, which feels wrong to most people but follows directly from the math — what matters is how many you sample, not what fraction of the whole they form (until the sample becomes a large share of a small population).

And the standing caveat: this buys precision only. It assumes honest random sampling; a biased frame or a 90% non-response rate makes the ±3 a fiction regardless of n.
I rolled a die 12 times and got three 6s. My friend says the die must be loaded — sixes are 'coming up too much'. Settle it.

Expected sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die: 12 x 1/6 = 2. You saw 3 — one extra. The probability that a perfectly fair die produces 3 or more sixes in 12 rolls is 1 - P(0) - P(1) - P(2) = 32%.

A 32% event is utterly ordinary — it happens in about one session in three. Your friend has confused 'more than expected' with 'more than chance allows'. With tiny samples, the count is dominated by luck: the standard deviation here is sqrt(12 x 1/6 x 5/6) = 1.3, so results from 0 to 4 sixes are all unremarkable.

If you genuinely suspect the die, the remedy is volume: roll it 600 times, where a fair die gives 100 sixes with a standard deviation of about 9 — a loaded die favouring sixes even slightly would stand out clearly. Suspicion is cheap; the sample size needed to confirm it is the real price of the claim.

An infographic compares oil production: Country A produces 2 million barrels a day and gets a barrel icon 2 cm tall. Country B produces 4 million and gets the same barrel icon drawn 4 cm tall and twice as wide. What's wrong?

The icon for B is scaled in both dimensions, so its area is 2 x 2 = 4 times A's area — for a value that is only 2 times bigger. Your eye reads area (and if the barrel is drawn with any depth, volume, which would be 8 times), so the graphic visually claims B produces four to eight times as much oil.

This is one of the oldest tricks in chart design, accidental or otherwise: when you scale a picture to represent a number, scale only one dimension, or better, repeat the icon (two barrels for B) so the count itself carries the value. The check to run on any pictogram: measure the areas, not the heights. If the area ratio doesn't match the value ratio, the chart is lying in proportion to the mismatch.

A headline calls Metro City 'the deadliest place to drive', citing 240 traffic deaths last year. Small City recorded 45 traffic deaths. Populations: Metro City 3,000,000; Small City 250,000. Compute the death rate per 100,000 residents for each and evaluate the headline.

Metro City: 240 / 3,000,000 x 100,000 = 8.0 deaths per 100,000 residents.
Small City: 45 / 250,000 x 100,000 = 18.0 deaths per 100,000 residents.

A resident of Small City faces 2.2 times the risk of a Metro City resident. The headline has it backwards because it compared raw counts between populations differing twelvefold in size.

Raw counts answer 'where do the most events happen?' — almost always 'where the most people are'. Risk questions require rates: events divided by the exposed population. This error drives real policy: resources get sent to big cities with the most incidents rather than small places with the worst rates. Whenever a comparison lacks a denominator, supply one before believing it.

A headline says a certain food additive 'increases the risk of a rare disease by 50%'. The study behind it found the disease in 4 out of every 100,000 people who avoid the additive and 6 out of every 100,000 who consume it. How worried should a consumer be?

The 50% is arithmetically true: 6 versus 4 per 100,000 is a 50% relative increase. But the absolute increase is 2 extra cases per 100,000 people — your personal risk moves from 0.004% to 0.006%.

Both framings describe the same data, and they produce opposite emotional responses, which is why press releases choose the relative one. The complete report of any risk change needs three numbers: the baseline rate, the new rate, and the difference in absolute terms. With those, you can weigh the risk against the hundred other risks of similar size you accept daily without thinking.

Note the symmetry: the same trick runs in reverse for benefits — a drug that cuts risk 'by 50%' from 2 in a million to 1 in a million is nearly worthless to an individual, while one that cuts it from 40% to 20% is major. Relative changes without base rates are advertising, not information.

A hospital tells patients '90 out of 100 people who have this surgery are alive five years later'. Another hospital, with identical outcomes, says '10 out of 100 patients die within five years'. Why do patients react differently, and which statement is more honest?

The statements are logically identical — 90 alive is 10 dead — but they frame the outcome on different reference points, and people evaluate gambles by the frame. '90 survive' foregrounds the gain and reliably makes the surgery more attractive; '10 die' foregrounds the loss and makes it less so. In classic experiments, this exact reframing shifted treatment choices substantially, including among physicians.

Neither statement is dishonest alone; the dishonesty is in choosing only one. The complete presentation gives both numbers ('90 of 100 alive, 10 of 100 dead') and, ideally, the same figures for the alternative treatments, since a decision is always between options, each with its own pair of numbers.

Practical defence: whenever you hear a single-framed statistic, mechanically restate it in the opposite frame before deciding. If your preference flips when the wording does, the preference was about the wording, not the outcome — and you should decide which outcome you actually want.
A slide shows a pie chart of 'apps people use daily': Messaging 45%, Social 40%, Music 25%, News 20%. A colleague objects that the pie is broken. Are they right?

Yes. The slices sum to 130% — more than a whole pie. The underlying survey clearly let people pick several apps, so these are percentages of respondents, not shares of a single whole.

A pie chart makes one promise: the slices partition something into parts that add to 100%. When the data are overlapping memberships, the pie visually invents a partition that doesn't exist — it implies, for instance, that messaging and social are separate territories when most people use both.
